newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Chechnya trade charges over bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Chechnya trade charges over bomb attack.

text.p: Recriminations over a fatal bomb attack raised tension between Russia and rebel Chechnya on Tuesday to their bitterest pitch since a cease-fire last August.

With peace talks between the two sides stalled, Russian police fought a brief night-time skirmish with a group of what they said were 20 Chechen fighters just outside Chechnya, resulting in casualties on both sides.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said police had detained two Chechen women fighters suspected of organising an explosion which killed two people and wounded more than 20 at a railway station in the south Russian spa resort of Pyatigorsk on Monday.

Kulikov, who is also a deputy prime minister, said the two were part of a Chechen armed group which attacked the Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995 and staged a bloody hostage drama in which more than 100 people were killed.
"These are not rebels. This is not a political struggle. This is banditry," Kulikov said. "We will catch and destroy those criminals."
The accusations were immediately denied by Chechen Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov, Itar-Tass news agency said.

The separatist leaders, who spearheaded a 21-month conflict with Russia that killed tens of thousands before last August's truce, accused unnamed Russian special services of planting the bomb to disrupt peacemaking.

"The leadership of the Chechen republic protests to the Russian authorities over the groundless accusations that the Chechen side was involved in the explosions at the railway stations," Tass quoted a statement by Chechen presidential spokesman Kazbek Khadzhiyev as saying.
A bomb explosion at Armavir railway station in southern Russia last Wednesday also killed two people.
The latest bout of tensions seemed to open differences both in Moscow and Grozny.
Russian news agencies reported that Udugov and a deputy head of the Russia's Security Council, Boris Berezovsky, agreed that peace talks should go ahead.
But Chechen vice-president Vakha Arsanov, quoted by Interfax news agency, said talks on political matters were impossible until Kulikov apologised for his allegations or proved them.
The cease-fire signed last August halted fighting but did not resolve the main dispute -- whether the rebel region is part of Russia or independent.

They two sides are now involved in difficult negotiations over a long-term peace treaty intended to open the way for Moscow's help in restoring Chechnya, where the capital and other towns were largely destroyed by Russian air and artillery attacks.
Berezovsky, heavily involved in shuttle diplomacy with Grozny, appealed for restraint.
"Irresponsible statements are being made today by those who have not had enough of the war in Chechnya," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

Kulikov, who commanded Russia's forces in Chechnya until he became interior minister in July 1995, said he feared Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov, a relative moderate elected in January, was losing control.
"It has become evident that there is no unity in the Chechen leadership and Maskhadov may be unable to control the situation," said Kulikov.
"If Maskhadov does not get rid of terrorists in his entourage, his regime will become a criminal one," he added.
Kulikov's remarks sounded similar to those which Moscow officials made late in 1994 on the eve of military intervention in Chechnya, which they called a haven for criminals.
President Boris Yeltsin, who has called the decision to use military force to quell Chechen separatists a mistake, was following the situation closely.
Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Tass the president was extremely concerned and wanted the law and order bodies to take the "most tough and resolute...actions".
